topics.name: Prime numbers
topics.kicker: Divisible only by 1 and themselves · The building blocks of arithmetic
topics.dates: Infinitely many, proved by Euclid c. 300 BCE
topics.briefing: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that can be divided evenly only by 1 and itself, like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11. Every other whole number above 1 can be built by multiplying primes together, so mathematicians call them the building blocks of arithmetic. Around 300 BCE, Euclid proved that the primes never run out, and many of the codes that protect online shopping depend on how hard it is to split huge numbers back into primes.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: While doodling during a long, dull talk at a 1963 scientific meeting, Stanisław Ulam [“OO-lahm”] wrote the counting numbers in a square spiral and noticed that these numbers tend to fall along diagonal lines. Leonhard Euler showed that the sum of the reciprocals of these numbers grows without limit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these whole numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, and 7, that are divisible only by 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: The narrator of Mark Haddon’s novel _The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time_ numbers his chapters using only these numbers. In Carl Sagan’s novel _Contact_, scientists realize that a radio signal from space was sent by intelligent beings because it counts out these numbers.
tossups.r: The number 2 is the only even one of them. For 10 points, name these numbers that have exactly two factors.

tossups.p: A $1 million Millennium Prize awaits whoever proves the Riemann hypothesis, which concerns how these numbers are spread out. In 1896, Jacques Hadamard [“ah-dah-MAR”] and Charles de la Vallée Poussin [“vah-LAY poo-SAN”] proved that the count of these numbers below n is roughly n divided by the natural log of n.
tossups.r: Every whole number above 1 is either one of these numbers or a product of them. For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, and 7.

tossups.p: In 2013, Yitang Zhang proved that infinitely many pairs of these numbers differ by less than 70 million. A still-unproven conjecture says there are infinitely many “twin” pairs of these numbers, such as 11 and 13, that differ by exactly 2.
tossups.r: The sieve of Eratosthenes [“air-uh-TOSS-thuh-neez”] finds these numbers. For 10 points, name these numbers whose only factors are 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: In 2024, a volunteer computer project called GIMPS found a record-setting one of these numbers with more than 41 million digits. Like most of the largest known examples, it has the form 2 to the n, minus 1, a type named for the French friar Marin Mersenne [“mair-SEN”].
tossups.r: Euclid proved that these numbers never run out. For 10 points, name these numbers, like 2, 3, 5, and 7, that are divisible only by 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: Christian Goldbach’s letters with Leonhard Euler in 1742 led to a still-unproven conjecture that every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two of these numbers. For example, 10 is 3 plus 7, and also 5 plus 5.
tossups.r: The only even one of these numbers is 2. For 10 points, name these numbers, like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11, whose only factors are 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: The RSA system, developed in 1977 by Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, keeps data secret because it is hard to find the two huge numbers of this type that were multiplied to build part of its key. Ordinary computers have no known fast way to split a number hundreds of digits long into these numbers.
tossups.r: Every whole number above 1 breaks into these numbers in only one way. For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, and 7.

tossups.p: Fermat’s little theorem says that if p is one of these numbers, then a to the p, minus a, is always a multiple of p. Fermat also guessed that 2 to the 32nd power, plus 1, was one of these numbers, but Leonhard Euler showed that it is divisible by 641.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, which include 2, 3, 5, and 7, that have exactly two factors.

tossups.p: Sophie Germain [“zhair-MAN”] studied numbers p of this type for which 2p plus 1 is also of this type, such as 11, because 23 is also one of them. A number of pennies of this type can be laid out in a rectangle only as a single row.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, like 2, 3, 5, and 7, whose only factors are 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: In Book IX of his _Elements_, Euclid proved that these numbers never run out. His proof multiplies a finite list of them together and adds 1, creating a number that none of the numbers on the list divide evenly.
tossups.r: A factor tree splits 12 into three of these numbers: 2, 2, and 3. For 10 points, name these numbers that have exactly two factors.

tossups.p: As a teenager, Carl Friedrich Gauss guessed how thinly these numbers are spread out among large numbers, a guess that was proven about a century later. Exactly 25 of these numbers are less than 100, and the largest of those is 97.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, and 7, that are divisible only by 1 and themselves.

tossups.p: Mathematicians decided that 1 is not one of these numbers so that every whole number above 1 has only one way to factor into them. Some biologists think certain cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground because cycles of these lengths rarely line up with the cycles of their predators.
tossups.r: The sieve of Eratosthenes [“air-uh-TOSS-thuh-neez”] finds these numbers by crossing out multiples. For 10 points, name these numbers, like 2, 3, 5, and 7.

tossups.p: Pafnuty Chebyshev [“cheh-bih-SHOFF”] proved Bertrand’s postulate, which says there is always at least one of these numbers between any whole number greater than 1 and twice that number. To test whether a number is one of these, you only need to try divisors up to its square root.
tossups.r: Whole numbers above 1 that are not of this type, like 4 and 9, are called composite. For 10 points, name these numbers, like 2, 3, 5, and 7, that have exactly two factors.

tossups.p: Ben Green and Terence Tao proved in 2004 that these numbers contain evenly spaced runs of any length, such as 5, 11, 17, 23, and 29. Eratosthenes [“air-uh-TOSS-thuh-neez”] names a “sieve” that finds these numbers by crossing out the multiples of 2, 3, 5, and so on.
tossups.r: Whole numbers above 1 that are not of this type are called composite. For 10 points, name these numbers that have exactly two factors.

tossups.p: Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”] proved that the list 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, and so on, which goes up by 4 each time, contains infinitely many of these numbers. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every whole number greater than 1 is a product of these numbers in exactly one way.
tossups.r: Two is the only even one of these numbers. For 10 points, name these numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11.

clues.t: Whole numbers greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and themselves, so each has exactly two factors
The list begins 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13; the number 2 is the only even one
Whole numbers above 1 that are not of this type, like 4, 6, 8, and 9, are called composite
A factor tree breaks a whole number into a product of them, such as 12 = 2 × 2 × 3
The sieve of Eratosthenes finds them by crossing out the multiples of 2, then of 3, then of 5, and so on
Euclid proved they never run out: multiply any finite list of them and add 1, and the result needs a new one as a factor
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every whole number above 1 is a product of them in exactly one way (ignoring order)
The number 1 is not one of them; leaving it out keeps every factorization unique
Goldbach’s conjecture (from letters with Euler, 1742): every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two of them; still unproven
Twin pairs differ by exactly 2, like 11 and 13; no one has proved there are infinitely many such pairs
Periodical cicadas come out every 13 or 17 years, and both 13 and 17 are of this type
RSA encryption (1977) keeps internet data secret because it is very hard to factor a product of two huge ones
To test a number, you only need to try dividing by whole numbers up to its square root
There are exactly 25 of them below 100; the largest is 97
Mersenne type: 2 to the n, minus 1, like 3, 7, 31, and 127 (n must also be one); named for the French friar Marin Mersenne
In 2024, the GIMPS volunteer search found a record-setting Mersenne one with more than 41 million digits
Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin proved (1896) that about n divided by the natural log of n of them are below n; Gauss guessed it as a teen
The Riemann hypothesis (1859), about how they are spread out, is unproven; a proof would win a $1 million Millennium Prize
Yitang Zhang proved in 2013 that infinitely many pairs of them differ by less than 70 million
Ulam spiral (1963): Stanisław Ulam doodled the counting numbers in a square spiral and saw these cluster on diagonal lines
Euler proved that the sum of their reciprocals, 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/5 + 1/7 + …, grows without limit
Fermat’s little theorem: if p is one of them, then a to the p, minus a, is always a multiple of p
Fermat guessed that 2 to the 32nd power, plus 1, was one of them, but Euler showed it is divisible by 641
Bertrand’s postulate, proved by Pafnuty Chebyshev: there is always one between any whole number n above 1 and 2n
A Sophie Germain one is a p for which 2p + 1 is also one, like 11 (because 23 qualifies too)
Green–Tao theorem (2004): they contain evenly spaced runs of any length, like 5, 11, 17, 23, 29
Dirichlet proved that lists like 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … (going up by 4) contain infinitely many of them
_The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time_ numbers its chapters only with them; in _Contact_, an alien signal counts them out

trap.title: Primes or their relatives?
trap.body: Some tossups ask for the opposite idea, composite numbers, which have more than two factors. Others want one special kind, such as Mersenne primes (2 to the n, minus 1) or twin primes, or the process called prime factorization. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite, so a question about 1 itself wants a different answer.
trap.fix: Listen to the giveaway. “Exactly two factors” or “divisible only by 1 and itself” means primes; “more than two factors” means composite numbers. If every clue is about 2 to the n, minus 1, or Marin Mersenne, say “Mersenne primes.”
trap.line: Real answer line: prime numbers (accept primes; do not accept “composite numbers”)

topics.name: Leonhard Euler
topics.kicker: Prolific Swiss mathematician · Popularized e, i, π, and f(x)
topics.briefing: Leonhard Euler [“OY-ler”] was a Swiss mathematician who wrote so much that his collected works fill dozens of thick volumes, and he kept working even after he went almost completely blind. He solved the puzzle of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg and popularized the symbols e, i, and π, along with f(x) for functions. His equation e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 is often called the most beautiful in mathematics.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Marquis de Condorcet [“kon-dor-SAY”] wrote that this man “ceased to calculate and to live” in 1783, on a day when he had been discussing the orbit of the newly discovered planet Uranus. This man kept producing mathematics after he went almost totally blind, by dictating to helpers.
tossups.r: His identity says e to the i pi, plus 1, equals 0. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician who solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem.

tossups.p: This man explained science to the public in his _Letters to a German Princess_, which used circle diagrams for logic long before John Venn did. He wrote those letters while working in Berlin for Frederick the Great, and he later returned to Saint Petersburg at the invitation of Catherine the Great.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician who showed that no walk could cross each of Königsberg’s seven bridges exactly once.

tossups.p: This man disproved a guess by Pierre de Fermat by showing that 2 to the 32nd power, plus 1, is divisible by 641. His totient function counts how many whole numbers up to n share no factor other than 1 with n.
tossups.r: He popularized the symbol pi and introduced the letter e for the base of the natural logarithm. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician.

tossups.p: This man became famous by solving the Basel problem, proving that the sum of 1, one-fourth, one-ninth, one-sixteenth, and so on forever equals pi squared over 6. Pierre-Simon Laplace [“luh-PLAHSS”] reportedly told students to read this man’s work, calling him “the master of us all.”
tossups.r: This man was the first to write f of x for a function. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician whose identity links e, i, pi, 1, and 0.

tossups.p: This man correctly guessed that 36 officers of six ranks from six regiments cannot be arranged in a 6-by-6 square with no rank or regiment repeated in any row or column. His 1736 book _Mechanica_ described motion using calculus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician whose polyhedron formula says that vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2.

tossups.p: In any triangle, the centroid, the orthocenter, and the circumcenter all lie on a straight line named for this man. He wrote a formula saying that e to the i x equals cosine x plus i times sine x.
tossups.r: This man solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem in 1736. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician.

tossups.p: This man and Lorenzo Mascheroni [“mah-skeh-ROH-nee”] name a constant, gamma, that is about 0.5772. This man’s father, a pastor, wanted him to study theology, but Johann Bernoulli [“ber-NOO-lee”] convinced his father that he should study mathematics instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician from Basel, Switzerland, who popularized the symbols e, i, and pi.

tossups.p: This man’s critical-load formula predicts the force that will make a slender column buckle, and his equations describe the flow of an ideal fluid with no viscosity. He showed that a cube’s 8 vertices, minus its 12 edges, plus its 6 faces equals 2.
tossups.r: His collected works fill dozens of volumes. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician who solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem.

tossups.p: This man’s portrait appeared on the Swiss 10-franc banknote. He introduced the letter i for the square root of negative 1 and the Greek letter sigma for a sum, and he made the symbol pi popular.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician who showed that no path could cross each of Königsberg’s seven bridges exactly once.

tossups.p: This man and Joseph-Louis Lagrange [“luh-GRAHNZH”] share an equation central to the calculus of variations. A simple step-by-step method for approximating solutions to differential equations is also named for this man.
tossups.r: In 1736, this man laid the foundations of graph theory with a puzzle about seven bridges. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician.

tossups.p: This man connected the prime numbers to the sum of 1 over n to the s by rewriting that sum as a product over all of the primes. He also proved that the sum of the reciprocals of the prime numbers grows without limit.
tossups.r: This man’s identity says e to the i pi, plus 1, equals 0. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician.

tossups.p: This man’s 1748 textbook _Introductio in analysin infinitorum_ made the idea of a function central to calculus, and he was the first to write f of x for a function. He spent his final 17 years in Saint Petersburg, Russia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician, for whom the number e, about 2.718, is often named.

tossups.p: Long before John Venn, this man drew overlapping and nested circles to explain logic, in diagrams now named after him. He also studied the knight’s tour, a path in which a chess knight visits every square of the board exactly once.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician whose identity says e to the i pi, plus 1, equals 0.

tossups.p: Three angles named for this man describe how a solid object is turned in space. A path that uses every edge of a network exactly once is named for this man; no such path exists if more than two points touch an odd number of edges.
tossups.r: This man solved the Basel problem and the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician.

tossups.p: Swiss scholars have spent more than a century publishing this man’s collected works, the _Opera Omnia_, which fill dozens of volumes. As a teenager, this man studied at the University of Basel under Johann Bernoulli [“ber-NOO-lee”].
tossups.r: He went almost totally blind but kept working. For 10 points, name this Swiss mathematician who popularized the symbols e, i, and pi.

clues.t: Swiss mathematician (1707–1783) from Basel who worked in St. Petersburg, Russia, and in Berlin, Prussia
Solved the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem (1736), the start of graph theory
His identity e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 links five key numbers: e, i, π, 1, and 0
The number e (about 2.718), the base of the natural log, is often called his number
Went almost totally blind late in life but kept working by dictating to helpers
Introduced or popularized the symbols f(x) for functions, e, i for the square root of −1, Σ for sums, and π
Polyhedron formula: vertices − edges + faces = 2 (for a cube, 8 − 12 + 6 = 2)
Solved the Basel problem: 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + … = π²/6
His formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x links exponents to sine and cosine
Studied under Johann Bernoulli in Basel; his father, a pastor, had wanted him to study theology
Worked for Frederick the Great in Berlin (1741–1766), then returned to Russia under Catherine the Great
Laplace reportedly told students to read him, because “he is the master of us all”
One of the most prolific mathematicians ever; his collected works, the _Opera Omnia_, fill dozens of volumes
Disproved Fermat’s guess that 2 to the 32nd power, plus 1, is a prime number by showing that 641 divides it
His totient function φ(n) counts the whole numbers up to n that share no factor (other than 1) with n
In any triangle, the centroid, orthocenter, and circumcenter lie on a straight line named for him
Shares the constant gamma (about 0.5772) with Lorenzo Mascheroni
_Letters to a German Princess_ explained science to everyday readers; its circle diagrams for logic came before Venn diagrams
Condorcet’s eulogy said he “ceased to calculate and to live” (1783)
On the day he died, he had been discussing the orbit of the newly discovered planet Uranus
His textbook _Introductio in analysin infinitorum_ (1748) made the function the central idea of calculus
A step-by-step method for approximating solutions to differential equations is named for him
Shares a key equation of the calculus of variations with Joseph-Louis Lagrange
His critical-load formula tells when a slender column will buckle; his equations also describe the flow of an ideal fluid
Thirty-six officers problem: he correctly guessed no 6 × 6 arrangement works, but his broader guess was disproved in 1959
Pictured on the Swiss 10-franc banknote; three angles that describe how a solid object is turned are named for him
A path that uses every edge of a network exactly once is named for him; none exists if more than two points touch an odd number of edges

trap.title: Euler or a Bernoulli?
trap.body: Euler grew up in Basel, studied under Johann Bernoulli, and worked in St. Petersburg alongside Daniel Bernoulli, so clues about Basel or St. Petersburg can also point to a Bernoulli. Jacob Bernoulli found the number e while studying compound interest, even though e is often called “Euler’s number.” Many tossups also want a concept tied to Euler, such as e or graph theory, rather than the man himself.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man” plus life clues: going blind, Frederick the Great, Catherine the Great, or writing f(x). Bernoulli clues usually mention probability, the law of large numbers, or Bernoulli’s principle about moving fluids.

topics.name: Fibonacci sequence
topics.kicker: Each number is the sum of the two before · 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…
topics.dates: Brought to Europe in Liber Abaci, 1202
topics.briefing: The Fibonacci sequence starts with 1 and 1, then keeps adding the last two numbers: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and on forever. Leonardo of Pisa, nicknamed Fibonacci, introduced this pattern to Europe in 1202 with a puzzle about breeding rabbits. Its numbers show up in the spirals of sunflowers and pinecones, and dividing each term by the one before it gets closer and closer to the golden ratio, about 1.618.
topics.answerHtml: Fibonacci sequence (accept Fibonacci numbers or Fibonacci series; prompt on sequence or recurrence relation)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Zeckendorf’s theorem says that every positive whole number can be written in exactly one way as a sum of terms of this sequence, using no two neighboring terms. Gabriel Lamé [“lah-MAY”] used neighboring terms of this sequence to find the slowest cases of the Euclidean algorithm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, in which each term is the sum of the two before it.

tossups.p: A puzzle that rearranges the four pieces of an 8-by-8 square into a 5-by-13 rectangle seems to gain one unit of area. Cassini’s identity explains the trick: the square of any term of this sequence differs by exactly 1 from the product of the two terms beside it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that Leonardo of Pisa used in a 1202 puzzle about breeding rabbits.

tossups.p: The last digits of the terms of this sequence repeat in a cycle of exactly 60 terms, an example of a Pisano [“pee-ZAH-noh”] period. Every fifth term of this sequence, such as 5, 55, and 610, is a multiple of 5.
tossups.r: Every third term of this sequence is even. For 10 points, name this sequence that goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

tossups.p: Édouard Lucas [“ay-DWAR loo-KAH”] gave this sequence its common name in the 1800s and studied a related sequence that begins 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11. Apart from 0 and 1, the only perfect square in this sequence is its 12th term, 144.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence in which each number, such as 13, is the sum of the two numbers before it, such as 5 and 8.

tossups.p: Centuries before Europeans studied it, Indian scholars such as Virahanka [“vee-ruh-HUN-kuh”] found this sequence by counting the rhythms that can be made from short and long syllables in Sanskrit poetry. Hemachandra [“hay-muh-CHUN-druh”] also described it around the year 1150.
tossups.r: In Europe, it appeared in the 1202 book _Liber Abaci_. For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

tossups.p: Leonardo of Pisa’s 1202 book _Liber Abaci_, which helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals across Europe, introduced this sequence with a puzzle whose answer was 377 pairs after one year. In that puzzle, each pair of animals produces a new pair every month, starting in its second month of life.
tossups.r: Those animals were rabbits. For 10 points, name this sequence in which each term is the sum of the two before it.

tossups.p: Tracing a male honeybee’s family tree back one generation at a time gives terms of this sequence, because male bees have only a mother. The spirals in a sunflower’s seed head often come in neighboring terms of this sequence, such as 34 and 55.
tossups.r: Each of its terms is the sum of the two before it. For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

tossups.p: The squares of this sequence’s first five terms, 1, 1, 4, 9, and 25, add up to 40, which equals its fifth term times its sixth term. Squares with side lengths from this sequence fit together into larger and larger rectangles and trace a spiral close to the golden spiral.
tossups.r: It begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. For 10 points, name this sequence in which each term is the sum of the previous two.

tossups.p: Adding up the numbers along the shallow diagonals of Pascal’s triangle produces the terms of this sequence. Every third term of this sequence, such as 2, 8, and 34, is even.
tossups.r: Its terms often appear in the spirals of pinecones and sunflowers. For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8.

tossups.p: In Dan Brown’s novel _The Da Vinci Code_, a scrambled list of numbers from this sequence is one of the first clues in a mystery. The ratios of neighboring terms of this sequence, such as 13 over 8 and 21 over 13, get closer and closer to the golden ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that Leonardo of Pisa introduced to Europe with a puzzle about rabbits.

tossups.p: A mathematics journal founded in 1963 is devoted entirely to this sequence and related ideas. This sequence’s name comes from a nickname meaning “son of Bonacci,” given to a man who learned Hindu-Arabic numerals as a boy in North Africa, where his father worked.
tossups.r: Each term is the sum of the two before it. For 10 points, name this sequence that goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21.

tossups.p: Many plants place each new seed or leaf about 137.5 degrees around from the one before, an arrangement that produces spiral counts from this sequence. Pinecones often show 8 spirals in one direction and 13 in the other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, in which each later term is the sum of the two before it.

tossups.p: Adding the first five terms of this sequence gives 12, which is one less than its seventh term, 13. In fact, the sum of its first n terms is always one less than the term two places later.
tossups.r: This sequence was named for Leonardo of Pisa. For 10 points, name this sequence that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.

tossups.p: Johannes Kepler noticed that dividing each term of this sequence by the term before it gets closer and closer to about 1.618. A rectangle whose sides are neighboring terms of this sequence, such as 13 by 21, is very close to a golden rectangle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence introduced to Europe by Leonardo of Pisa, in which each term is the sum of the previous two.

tossups.p: Although it is named for Jacques Binet [“bee-NAY”], a formula that gives any term of this sequence directly, using powers of the golden ratio and the square root of 5, was known earlier to Abraham de Moivre [“duh MWAHV”]. This sequence’s 10th term is 55.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence, which begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, named for Leonardo of Pisa.

clues.t: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34…
Named for the nickname of Leonardo of Pisa, an Italian mathematician of the early 1200s
Introduced to Europe with a puzzle about how fast a population of rabbits grows
Dividing each term by the one before (8/5, 13/8, 21/13…) gets closer and closer to the golden ratio, about 1.618
Spiral counts in sunflowers, pinecones, and pineapples are often its terms
Appeared in Leonardo’s book _Liber Abaci_ (1202), which also helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals across Europe
Recurrence rule F(n) = F(n − 1) + F(n − 2), often starting with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1
Every third term is even (2, 8, 34…), and every fifth term is a multiple of 5 (5, 55, 610…)
Adding the numbers along the shallow diagonals of Pascal’s triangle gives its terms
A male honeybee’s family tree has 1 parent, 2 grandparents, 3 great-grandparents, then 5, 8… ancestors per generation going back
Squares with its terms as side lengths fit into rectangles and trace a spiral close to the golden spiral
Indian scholars of Sanskrit poetry knew it before Leonardo: Virahanka centuries earlier, and Hemachandra around 1150
In Dan Brown’s _The Da Vinci Code_, a scrambled list of its terms is one of the first clues in the mystery
Johannes Kepler noticed that ratios of neighboring terms approach the golden ratio
Binet’s formula gives any term directly from powers of the golden ratio and √5; Abraham de Moivre knew it earlier
Édouard Lucas gave it its common name in the 1800s; his Lucas numbers 2, 1, 3, 4, 7, 11… follow the same rule
Cassini’s identity: a term squared differs by exactly 1 from the product of its two neighbors (8 × 8 = 64; 5 × 13 = 65)
A puzzle rearranges the pieces of an 8 × 8 square into a 5 × 13 rectangle and seems to gain one unit of area
Zeckendorf’s theorem: every positive whole number is a sum of non-neighboring terms in exactly one way
The last digits of its terms repeat in a cycle of 60 (a Pisano period)
Gabriel Lamé used neighboring terms to find the slowest cases of the Euclidean algorithm
A mathematics journal founded in 1963, a “Quarterly,” is devoted entirely to it
Its 12th term is 144 = 12 × 12; apart from 0 and 1, 144 is its only perfect square
The squares of its first terms add up to a product of two neighbors: 1 + 1 + 4 + 9 + 25 = 40 = 5 × 8
The sum of its first n terms is one less than the term two places later: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 12 = 13 − 1
The nickname means “son of Bonacci”; Leonardo learned Hindu-Arabic numerals as a boy in North Africa, where his father worked
Leonardo’s original rabbit puzzle ended with 377 pairs after one year
Plants that place each new seed about 137.5° around from the last (the golden angle) produce its spiral counts

trap.title: Sequence, ratio, or man?
trap.body: Three answer lines sit very close together. The golden ratio (about 1.618, also called phi) is the number that neighboring terms of this sequence approach. Leonardo of Pisa is the man, who also helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe, and Lucas numbers follow the same adding rule but start 2, 1.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This sequence” or “these numbers” means Fibonacci; “this ratio” or “this constant,” with clues about regular pentagons or phi, means the golden ratio; “this mathematician,” with clues about his life and _Liber Abaci_, means Fibonacci the man.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fibonacci sequence (accept Fibonacci numbers or Fibonacci series; prompt on sequence or recurrence relation)

topics.name: Trigonometric functions
topics.kicker: Sine, cosine, tangent, and their kin · Turn angles into ratios
topics.dates: First known chord tables by Hipparchus, 2nd century BCE
topics.briefing: Trigonometric functions turn an angle into a number. In a right triangle, the sine of an angle is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent, which students remember as SOH-CAH-TOA. The astronomer Hipparchus built the first known table of chords, their ancestor, more than 2,000 years ago, and the same functions describe sound waves, tides, and anything else that repeats in cycles.
topics.answerHtml: trigonometric functions (accept trig functions, trigonometric ratios, or circular functions; prompt on trigonometry or functions; do not accept a single function like “sine”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Madhava [“MAH-duh-vuh”] of Sangamagrama and the Kerala school found infinite series for some of these functions centuries before European mathematicians did. One of these functions equals x minus x cubed over 3 factorial, plus x to the fifth over 5 factorial, and so on.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine, that relate angles to side ratios in right triangles.

tossups.p: The name of one of these functions comes from a Latin word for “fold” or “bay,” a mistranslation of an Arabic word that came from the Sanskrit word jya [“JYAH”], meaning “bowstring.” Aryabhata [“AR-yuh-BAH-tuh”] made an early table of values for that function in 499 CE.
tossups.r: Students remember three of them with the mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA. For 10 points, name these functions, including sine, cosine, and tangent.

tossups.p: Regiomontanus [“ree-jee-oh-mon-TAY-nus”] wrote one of the first European books about these functions, _On Triangles of All Kinds_, and Bartholomaeus Pitiscus [“pih-TISS-kus”] coined the name of the field that studies them in 1595. Hipparchus [“hih-PAR-kus”] made the first known table of chords, an ancestor of these functions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine, that relate the angles and sides of right triangles.

tossups.p: A formula named for Abraham de Moivre [“duh MWAHV”] raises a complex number written using two of these functions to any whole-number power. Euler’s formula says that e to the i x equals one of these functions of x plus i times another.
tossups.r: The graphs of two of them are waves that repeat every 360 degrees. For 10 points, name these functions, which include sine and cosine.

tossups.p: While studying how heat flows, Joseph Fourier [“FOOR-ee-ay”] showed how to build complicated repeating signals by adding up waves described by two of these functions. A mass bouncing on a spring moves in simple harmonic motion, which these functions also describe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine, whose values for an angle come from the sides of a right triangle.

tossups.p: Hyperbolic versions of these functions, built from powers of e, describe the curve of a hanging chain, called a catenary [“KAT-uh-nair-ee”]. In calculus, the derivative of one of these functions is another one of them, and the derivative of that second function is the negative of the first.
tossups.r: Two of their graphs are repeating waves that never go above 1 or below negative 1. For 10 points, name these functions, including sine, cosine, and tangent.

tossups.p: Navigators used the haversine formula, built from these functions, to find distances between two points on Earth’s surface. For very small angles measured in radians, one of these functions is almost equal to the angle itself, a shortcut used in the math of pendulums.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions whose values can be read off the unit circle, such as sine and cosine.

tossups.p: A law named for one of these functions says that c squared equals a squared plus b squared, minus 2ab times that function of angle C. Another law says that, in any triangle, each side divided by one of these functions of its opposite angle gives the same value.
tossups.r: Those laws help solve triangles that have no right angle. For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine.

tossups.p: The squares of two of these functions of the same angle always add up to 1, an identity that comes from the Pythagorean theorem. Another of these functions repeats every 180 degrees and is undefined at 90 degrees.
tossups.r: That function, tangent, equals opposite over adjacent. For 10 points, name these functions, which also include sine and cosine.

tossups.p: The “co-” in the names of three of these functions stands for “complement,” since each one’s value for an angle equals a partner’s value for 90 degrees minus that angle. Two others are named from Latin words meaning “touching” and “cutting.”
tossups.r: The basic three are remembered with SOH-CAH-TOA. For 10 points, name these six functions, including sine and cosine.

tossups.p: Ptolemy’s _Almagest_ included a table of chords that astronomers used much as later scientists used tables of these functions. On the unit circle, the x- and y-coordinates of the point at a given angle are two of these functions of that angle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions, including sine and cosine, often remembered with the mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA.

tossups.p: According to a double-angle identity, one of these functions of 2x equals 2 times that function of x times another of these functions of x. Two of these functions have wave-shaped graphs that repeat every 360 degrees, or 2 pi radians.
tossups.r: Those two waves never rise above 1 or fall below negative 1. For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine.

tossups.p: The inverses of these functions, which turn a ratio back into an angle, have names that begin with the prefix “arc.” Calculators must be set to degrees or radians before they compute these functions.
tossups.r: Surveyors use them to find heights from a distance and an angle. For 10 points, name these functions, which include sine, cosine, and tangent.

tossups.p: A tuning fork’s pure tone and the voltage of household alternating current both rise and fall in waves described by these functions. One of these functions equals the ratio of two others and has vertical asymptotes at 90 degrees and 270 degrees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these functions, such as sine and cosine, whose ratios students remember with SOH-CAH-TOA.

tossups.p: Snell’s law of refraction says that a material’s refractive index times one of these functions of the ray’s angle stays the same as light passes into a new material. In polar coordinates, x equals r times one of these functions of theta, and y equals r times another.
tossups.r: They relate the angles of a right triangle to ratios of its sides. For 10 points, name these functions, including sine and cosine.

clues.t: SOH-CAH-TOA: sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent
They relate an angle in a right triangle to ratios of the triangle’s side lengths
There are six: sine, cosine, tangent, and their reciprocals cosecant, secant, and cotangent
On the unit circle, the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ); in polar coordinates, x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ
Graphs of sine and cosine are repeating waves whose values stay between −1 and 1
Pythagorean identity: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 for every angle
Key values: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 45° = 1, and sin 90° = 1
Periodic: sine and cosine repeat every 360° (2π radians), while tangent repeats every 180°
Tangent equals sine divided by cosine, so it is undefined at 90° and 270°
Law of Sines: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C; Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C, for any triangle
Their inverses, such as arcsine and arctangent, turn a ratio back into an angle
In calculus, the derivative of sin x is cos x, and the derivative of cos x is −sin x
Hipparchus (2nd century BCE) made the first known table of chords, the ancestor of these functions
Simple harmonic motion, household AC voltage, and a tuning fork’s pure tone all follow sine-shaped waves
Euler’s formula: e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x
De Moivre’s formula: (cos x + i sin x) to the nth power = cos nx + i sin nx
Joseph Fourier, studying heat flow, showed how to build repeating signals by adding sine and cosine waves
Taylor series: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
Madhava of Sangamagrama and the Kerala school found infinite series for sine and cosine centuries before Europeans
“Sine” comes from Latin sinus (“fold” or “bay”), a mistranslation of an Arabic word from Sanskrit jya (“bowstring”), used in Aryabhata’s 499 CE table
The “co-” in cosine, cotangent, and cosecant means “complement”; tangent and secant come from Latin for “touching” and “cutting”
Ptolemy’s _Almagest_ included a table of chords for astronomy
Regiomontanus wrote _On Triangles of All Kinds_; Bartholomaeus Pitiscus coined the name of the field in 1595
Hyperbolic versions (sinh, cosh) are built from powers of e; a hanging chain forms a cosh-shaped curve called a catenary
For small angles measured in radians, sin x is very close to x, a shortcut used for pendulums
Navigators used the haversine formula to find distances between points on Earth’s surface
Double-angle identity: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x
Snell’s law of refraction: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

trap.title: One function or the family?
trap.body: Many tossups want a single function instead of the whole family: sine (opposite over hypotenuse), cosine (adjacent over hypotenuse), or tangent (opposite over adjacent). A tossup that asks for “this function” wants one name, while “these functions” wants the group. Giving the family name when one function is wanted can cost you the tossup.
trap.fix: Match the ratio in the giveaway: opposite ÷ hypotenuse is sine, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is cosine, and opposite ÷ adjacent is tangent. If the question says “these functions” or “six functions,” say “trigonometric functions.”
trap.line: Real answer line: trigonometric functions (accept trig functions, trigonometric ratios, or circular functions; prompt on trigonometry or functions; do not accept a single function like “sine”)

topics.name: Euclid
topics.kicker: Greek “father of geometry” · Author of the Elements
topics.briefing: Around 300 BCE in Alexandria, Egypt, a Greek mathematician named Euclid gathered the geometry of his time into one great work, the _Elements_. Starting from a list of definitions and five basic assumptions called postulates, he proved hundreds of facts step by step, from drawing an equilateral triangle to showing that the prime numbers never run out. Students learned geometry from his book for more than 2,000 years, which is why he is called the “father of geometry.”

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Edna St. Vincent Millay wrote a sonnet claiming that this man “alone has looked on Beauty bare.” Abraham Lincoln studied the first six books of this man’s most famous work to learn what it means to “demonstrate” something.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician from Alexandria who wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: According to one story, when a student asked what he would gain from learning geometry, this teacher had a servant give the student a coin, since the student wanted to profit from what he learned. This man supposedly told a king that “there is no royal road to geometry.”
tossups.r: That king was Ptolemy I of Egypt. For 10 points, name this “father of geometry,” who wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: Oliver Byrne’s 1847 edition of this man’s greatest work replaced the letters in its diagrams with brightly colored shapes. That work’s first printed edition appeared in Venice in 1482, and its first English translation, by Henry Billingsley, appeared in 1570.
tossups.r: That work’s first proposition shows how to draw an equilateral triangle with a compass and straightedge. For 10 points, name this author of the _Elements_.

tossups.p: Adelard of Bath translated this man’s most famous book from Arabic into Latin in the 1100s. That book is often said to have been printed in more editions than any other book except the Bible.
tossups.r: That book proves the Pythagorean theorem near the end of its first part. For 10 points, name this Greek author of the _Elements_.

tossups.p: Much of the little that is known about this man’s life comes from a commentary written by Proclus [“PROH-klus”] more than 700 years after he lived. Medieval writers sometimes confused this man with a philosopher of the same name from Megara who studied with Socrates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician who worked in Alexandria around 300 BCE and wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: The longest of the 13 books in this man’s major work deals with irrational lengths, and its fifth book presents a theory of proportion credited to Eudoxus [“yoo-DOK-sus”]. Its final book shows how to construct the five Platonic solids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician whose _Elements_ was the standard geometry textbook for centuries.

tossups.p: This man’s lemma states that if a prime number divides a product of two whole numbers, it must divide at least one of them. His formula builds Pythagorean triples, such as 3, 4, and 5, from two whole numbers m and n.
tossups.r: This man also proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers. For 10 points, name this Greek geometer who wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: In Book IX of his best-known work, this man showed how to build a perfect number, such as 28, from a prime number, such as 7, that is one less than a power of 2. That same book contains his proof that the prime numbers never run out.
tossups.r: He is called the “father of geometry.” For 10 points, name this Alexandrian mathematician whose _Elements_ starts from five postulates.

tossups.p: Nikolai Lobachevsky [“loh-buh-CHEF-skee”] and János Bolyai [“BOH-yoy”] built new geometries by rejecting the fifth postulate of this man. A modern version of that postulate, Playfair’s axiom, says that through a point not on a given line, only one parallel line can be drawn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician whose fifth postulate is called the parallel postulate.

tossups.p: Besides his most famous book, this man wrote _Optics_, about how we see objects; _Phaenomena_ [“fee-NOM-ih-nuh”], about astronomy; and _Data_, about what can be worked out from given facts in geometry problems. His books on conic sections have been lost.
tossups.r: This man’s algorithm finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers. For 10 points, name this author of the _Elements_.

tossups.p: In Raphael’s painting _The School of Athens_, a figure bending over a slate with a compass is often identified as this man. A European space telescope launched in 2023 to study dark matter and dark energy is named after him.
tossups.r: He wrote the _Elements_. For 10 points, name this mathematician known as the “father of geometry.”

tossups.p: Proposition 5 of this man’s first book, which proves that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, is nicknamed the pons asinorum [“ponz ah-sih-NOR-um”], or “bridge of donkeys,” because weaker students struggled to get past it.
tossups.r: This man proved the Pythagorean theorem as Proposition 47 of the same book. For 10 points, name this author of the _Elements_.

tossups.p: This man’s first definition says that a point is “that which has no part.” He listed common notions such as “things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another” after giving 23 definitions at the start of his first book.
tossups.r: His five postulates included one about parallel lines. For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician who wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: Proposition 2 of the seventh book of this man’s major work finds the largest number that divides two given numbers, using a method of repeated subtraction now named after him. That method is one of the oldest algorithms still in common use.
tossups.r: He is called the “father of geometry.” For 10 points, name this Greek mathematician from Alexandria who wrote the _Elements_.

tossups.p: Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi [“shoo gwahng-CHEE”] translated the first six books of this man’s most famous work into Chinese in 1607. That work’s first proposition shows how to build an equilateral triangle using only a compass and a straightedge.
tossups.r: That work starts from five postulates. For 10 points, name this Greek author of the _Elements_.

clues.t: Greek mathematician known as the “father of geometry”
Wrote the _Elements_, a geometry textbook in 13 books that was used for more than 2,000 years
Worked in Alexandria, Egypt, around 300 BCE, in the time of King Ptolemy I
Built geometry from definitions, five postulates, and common notions like “things equal to the same thing are equal to one another”
His fifth postulate is the parallel postulate; Lobachevsky and Bolyai built new geometries by rejecting it
Reportedly told King Ptolemy I that “there is no royal road to geometry”
Proved that there are infinitely many prime numbers (_Elements_, Book IX)
His algorithm finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers (_Elements_, Book VII)
Book I, Proposition 47 proves the Pythagorean theorem; Proposition 48 proves its converse
Book I, Proposition 1: build an equilateral triangle on a segment using only a compass and straightedge
Book XIII, the last book of the _Elements_, constructs the five Platonic solids
The _Elements_ is often said to have had more editions than any book except the Bible
A European space telescope launched in 2023 to study dark matter and dark energy is named for him
Abraham Lincoln studied the first six books of the _Elements_ to learn what it means to “demonstrate” something
When a student asked what he would gain from geometry, he reportedly had a servant give the student a coin
Edna St. Vincent Millay’s sonnet says he “alone has looked on Beauty bare”
The _Elements_ was first printed in Venice in 1482 and first put into English in 1570; Oliver Byrne’s 1847 edition used colored shapes instead of letters
Adelard of Bath translated the _Elements_ from Arabic into Latin in the 1100s
Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi translated its first six books into Chinese in 1607
Proclus’s commentary, written over 700 years later, is a main source on his life; medieval writers confused him with a philosopher from Megara
Also wrote _Optics_, _Data_, and _Phaenomena_ (about astronomy); his books on conic sections are lost
Book X, the longest book of the _Elements_, deals with irrational lengths; Book V’s theory of proportion comes from Eudoxus
Book I, Proposition 5 (the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal) is nicknamed the pons asinorum, “bridge of donkeys”
His lemma: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors; his formula makes Pythagorean triples like 3, 4, 5
Showed how to build an even perfect number, like 28 = 4 × 7, from a prime that is one less than a power of 2
Often identified as the figure bending over a slate with a compass in Raphael’s _The School of Athens_

trap.title: The man or his work?
trap.body: Several answer lines grow out of this one. Some tossups want his book, the _Elements_; others want the parallel postulate, his algorithm for the greatest common divisor, or geometry itself. The Pythagorean theorem is proved in the _Elements_ but is named for Pythagoras, and Leonhard Euler is a different mathematician who lived about 2,000 years later.
trap.fix: Listen for “this man” or “this mathematician” versus “this work,” “this postulate,” or “this method.” Clues about Alexandria, Ptolemy I, a coin given to a student, or the “father of geometry” mean the man.

topics.name: Triangles
topics.kicker: Three sides, three angles · Angles add up to 180° on a flat surface
topics.dates: Angle-sum proof in Euclid’s Elements, c. 300 BCE
topics.briefing: A triangle is the simplest polygon: three straight sides, three corners, and three angles that always add up to 180 degrees on a flat surface. Triangles are sorted by their sides (equilateral, isosceles, or scalene) and by their angles (acute, right, or obtuse), and the Pythagorean theorem works only for right triangles. Engineers build bridges and towers from triangles because, unlike a square, a triangle cannot be pushed out of shape without changing the length of a side.
topics.answerHtml: triangles (accept specific kinds, such as equilateral triangles; prompt on polygons or shapes)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Frank Morley discovered in 1899 that, in any one of these shapes, the angle trisectors nearest each side meet at the corners of a smaller, equilateral one. The point where the three angle bisectors of one of these shapes meet is the center of its inscribed circle.
tossups.r: Each of these shapes has three sides. For 10 points, name these polygons whose three interior angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322, made around 1800 BCE, contains columns of numbers that come from whole-number side lengths of right-angled examples of these shapes. In those examples, the side across from the right angle is the longest side, called the hypotenuse.
tossups.r: The Pythagorean theorem applies to right examples of these shapes. For 10 points, name these three-sided polygons.

tossups.p: Franz Reuleaux [“roo-LOH”] names a rounded version of the equilateral one of these shapes that has the same width in every direction, like a circle. Drill bits shaped that way can drill holes that are almost square.
tossups.r: Equilateral examples of these shapes have three 60-degree angles. For 10 points, name these polygons with three sides.

tossups.p: Wacław Sierpiński [“VAHTS-wahf sher-PEEN-skee”] names a fractal made by splitting one of these shapes into four smaller copies and removing the middle one, over and over. The same pattern appears when the odd numbers in the number arrangement named for Blaise Pascal are shaded.
tossups.r: Each one has three sides. For 10 points, name these shapes, which can be equilateral, isosceles, or scalene.

tossups.p: Viviani’s theorem says that from any point inside an equilateral one of these shapes, the distances to the three sides add up to its height. The Fermat point of one of these shapes is the spot with the smallest total distance to its three corners.
tossups.r: They have three sides. For 10 points, name these polygons whose area equals one-half times base times height.

tossups.p: Karl Feuerbach [“FOY-er-bahk”] proved that a circle passing through nine special points of one of these shapes touches the circle inscribed inside it. Those nine points include the midpoints of the shape’s sides and the feet of its altitudes.
tossups.r: An equilateral one of these shapes has three equal sides. For 10 points, name these shapes whose angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter of one of these shapes always lie on a line named for Leonhard Euler, but the incenter usually does not. The centroid, where the three medians meet, is the balance point of one of these shapes.
tossups.r: These shapes can be acute, right, or obtuse. For 10 points, name these three-sided polygons.

tossups.p: Heron of Alexandria gave a formula for the area of one of these shapes that uses only its three side lengths. Thales [“THAY-leez”] is credited with showing that if one of these shapes has all three corners on a circle and one side is a diameter, the angle opposite that side is a right angle.
tossups.r: The area of one of these shapes is half its base times its height. For 10 points, name these polygons with three sides.

tossups.p: M. C. Escher’s print _Waterfall_ uses an impossible version of this shape that was popularized by Lionel and Roger Penrose. On the surface of a sphere, the three angles of this shape add up to more than 180 degrees.
tossups.r: On a flat surface, they add up to exactly 180 degrees. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: A theorem credited to Napoleon Bonaparte says that if equilateral versions of this shape are built outward on the sides of any one of them, their centers form another equilateral one. The first proposition of Euclid’s _Elements_ constructs an equilateral one.
tossups.r: This shape can be acute, right, or obtuse. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: Knowing two sides of this shape and an angle that is not between them can describe two different examples of it, which is why “SSA” cannot prove that two of them are congruent. The shortcuts SSS, SAS, and ASA do work.
tossups.r: Two of these with matching angles are similar. For 10 points, name this polygon whose three angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: Three of the five Platonic solids, the tetrahedron, the octahedron, and the icosahedron, have faces in this shape. Equilateral versions of this shape are one of only three regular polygons that can tile a flat surface with no gaps, along with squares and hexagons.
tossups.r: Its area is one-half times base times height. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: The name of one type of this shape comes from Greek words meaning “equal legs,” and Euclid’s proof that its two base angles are equal was nicknamed the “bridge of donkeys.” Bridge trusses are built from this shape because it is rigid.
tossups.r: It is the polygon with the fewest sides. For 10 points, name this shape, which can be equilateral, isosceles, or scalene.

tossups.p: One special right example of this shape has angles of 30, 60, and 90 degrees and sides in the ratio 1 to the square root of 3 to 2. Any exterior angle of this shape equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.
tossups.r: This shape has three sides. For 10 points, name this polygon whose three angles always add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The name of the branch of math that studies the sides and angles of this shape comes from the Greek words for it and for “measure.” According to an inequality named for this shape, the lengths of any two of its sides must add up to more than the third.
tossups.r: Its angles add up to 180 degrees. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon, whose right-angled versions obey the Pythagorean theorem.

clues.t: A polygon with three sides, three vertices, and three angles; the polygon with the fewest sides
On a flat surface, its three interior angles always add up to 180 degrees
By sides: equilateral (all three equal), isosceles (at least two equal), or scalene (none equal)
By angles: acute (all under 90°), right (one exactly 90°), or obtuse (one over 90°)
Area = one-half × base × height
Right ones obey the Pythagorean theorem, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse
Equilateral ones have three 60° angles, making them the regular three-sided polygon
Any two sides added together must be longer than the third side (an inequality named for this shape)
Congruence shortcuts SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS work, but SSA does not; two with matching angles are similar, with sides in proportion
They are rigid, which is why bridge trusses and bicycle frames are built from them
Heron’s formula finds the area from the three side lengths, using half the perimeter (the semiperimeter)
Centers: centroid (medians), circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors), incenter (angle bisectors), orthocenter (altitudes)
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
Special right ones: 30-60-90 (sides 1 : √3 : 2) and 45-45-90 (sides 1 : 1 : √2)
The centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter always lie on the Euler line; the incenter usually does not
The nine-point circle passes through the side midpoints and the feet of the altitudes; Feuerbach showed it touches the inscribed circle
Napoleon’s theorem: build equilateral ones outward on the sides of any one, and their centers form another equilateral one
Morley’s theorem (discovered 1899): in any one, the angle trisectors nearest each side meet at the corners of an equilateral one
Viviani’s theorem: in an equilateral one, distances from any inside point to the sides add up to its height; the Fermat point minimizes total distance to the corners
Wacław Sierpiński’s 1915 fractal removes the middle one of four smaller copies, again and again
The Reuleaux shape, a rounded version of the equilateral one, has the same width in every direction
An impossible version, popularized by Lionel and Roger Penrose, appears in M. C. Escher’s print _Waterfall_
On a sphere, the angles add up to more than 180°; in hyperbolic geometry, to less than 180°
Thales’ theorem: if all three corners are on a circle and one side is a diameter, the angle opposite it is a right angle
The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 (about 1800 BCE) holds numbers from whole-number sides of right ones
Equilateral ones tile a flat surface (as squares and hexagons do) and form the faces of the tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron
“Isosceles” is Greek for “equal legs”; Euclid’s proof that its base angles are equal is the pons asinorum, “bridge of donkeys”
The math of their sides and angles is named from Greek words for this shape and “measure”

trap.title: Any shape or one kind?
trap.body: Some tossups want one specific kind: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (at least two equal sides), scalene (no equal sides), or right (one 90° angle). On those, plain “triangle” may earn only a prompt, so be ready to add the type. Other tossups want the Pythagorean theorem, which works only for right ones, or Pascal’s triangle, which is a pattern of numbers rather than a shape.
trap.fix: Listen to the giveaway. If it says “three-sided polygon” with clues true of every one (angles add up to 180°, area is one-half × base × height), say “triangle.” If it gives a defining detail like “all three sides equal” or “one 90-degree angle,” name that kind.
